precipice

PRES-ih-pis -- from Latin praeceps, 'steep, headlong,' ultimately from caput, 'head.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Precipice is the edge or brink of a very steep, dangerous drop, often used figuratively for the brink of disaster.

After a third year of shrinking donations, the community theater stood on the precipice of closing its doors for good.

Worked Example

The small publishing house had one book left on its schedule, no more funding, and a landlord threatening eviction within the month.

Standing right at the edge of total collapse, with disaster one small step away, is exactly what it means to be on a precipice.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

cliff-edge: A cliff-edge is the very edge of a literal steep drop, and in writing it mostly works as a describing word -- a cliff-edge moment, cliff-edge talks. Precipice does the same job as a noun in its own right, and it slips easily into figurative use for looming disaster.

verge: Verge means the point just before something happens, good or bad -- the verge of tears, the verge of a solution. Precipice paints a steep, deadly drop, so it fits only situations sliding toward disaster, never happy arrivals.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

safety: the state of being free from danger

stability: the state of being firmly fixed and unlikely to change or fail

Where it sits · how dangerous the drop ahead is — brink → precipice → chasm

brink vs. precipice: Brink is a common, everyday word for the edge of almost anything, good or bad -- the brink of a discovery, the brink of tears. Precipice is more dramatic and almost always negative, picturing an actual steep drop just ahead.

chasm vs. precipice: A chasm is graver than a precipice: a precipice is the edge where you might still step back, while a chasm is the vast drop itself -- once something falls in, there is no climbing out.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pre-

prefix — pre-: before, forward (Latin (prae-))

root — -cip-

root — -cip-: head (as in headlong, steep) (Latin (caput, 'head'))

suffix — -ice

suffix — -ice: forming a noun (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Precipice comes from Latin praeceps, 'headlong, steep' -- pre- ('forward') plus caput ('head') -- with -ice forming the noun. Standing on a precipice literally pictures going head-first over a steep edge.

Use the root in a new word: capital

Use the root in a new word: capital: Because the shipwreck cost the company its entire capital, the owners had to close the shop for good.
